By reformulating the problem in a commuting momentum space, the coordinates can be represented as linear differential operators $\hat x_a = -i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p) \partial /\partial p_b$. The matrix $E_{ab}(p)$ represents an infinite series involving the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H = -\frac 12 \hat D_a^2$ describes motion along group manifolds with characteristic size $\theta^{-1}$. The metrics of these manifolds are also expressed as infinite series in $\theta$, with $E_{ab}$ acting as vielbeins. For $su(2)$ and $u(N)$ algebras, it has been possible to express the operators $\hat x_a$ in simple finite forms. This study has led to new nonstandard formulas for the metrics of spheres $S^n$, projective spaces $RP^n$, and $U(2)$.

A major challenge for achieving reliable data transmission in this system is the distortion caused by chromatic dispersion, resulting in four spectral nulls in the signal. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer is employed, but its effectiveness is limited due to the propagation of burst errors. A weighted DFE can mitigate this issue, but its performance is further enhanced when combined with maximum likelihood sequence estimation. Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy.

Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. massive arc-like structure on the sky at a redshift of approximately 0.8. Spanning nearly 1 gigaparsec in size, this structure, known as the Giant Arc, appears almost symmetrical on the sky and was discovered through the presence of magnesium II absorbers in the spectra of background quasars. Utilizing magnesium II absorbers offers a novel approach to investigating large-scale structures at redshifts between 0.45 and 2.25. We present the observational characteristics of the Giant Arc and evaluate its statistical significance using three distinct methods: hierarchical clustering, the Cuzick-Edwards test, and power spectrum analysis. Each of these approaches has unique attributes and provides compelling evidence when considered collectively. To address potential biases in our analysis, we employed strategies to mitigate post-discovery significance assessments. Our findings indicate that the Giant Arc exhibits an overdensity of approximately 1.3, with a margin of error of 0.3. This structure is part of a growing collection of massive large-scale structures that may challenge the cosmological principle, which underlies the standard model of cosmology. The Giant Arc could be a precursor to a structure like the Sloan Great Wall, but on a much larger scale, observed when the universe was half its current age.

Two primary approaches, direct methods and two-stage pipelines, can be distinguished based on whether intermediate cues are employed. In the latter category, CNNs first regress intermediate cues such as 3D object coordinates or virtual control points in the initial stage. These intermediate cues then facilitate the computation of object pose through constructed correspondence constraints. This paper focuses on refining two-stage pipelines by integrating two distinct concepts: projection grouping and correspondence learning. We begin by utilizing a local patch-based method to generate projection heatmaps, representing the confidence distribution of projected 3D bounding box corners. A projection grouping module is then introduced to eliminate redundant local maxima from heatmaps. In contrast to directly applying the perspective-n-point (PnP) algorithm, multiple correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and their neighborhoods, and ranked by a correspondence-evaluation network. Ultimately, the proposed framework selects correspondences with higher confidence to determine object pose, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods in extensive experiments on three public datasets.

Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world physics. This paper delves into the aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a thorough examination of the theory and its numerical representations. Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits. A closer examination was conducted on the role of non-locality in determining motion, the interplay between kernel structure and material non-penetration, as well as the influence of PD kernel non-linearity on predicting fracture development. Finally, an exploration is initiated on adapting BB-PD to model fluids within the context of fading memory materials, suggesting directions for enhanced understanding of fluid dynamics through peridynamics.

This library builds upon the Graphical Lasso method, initially introduced in (Friedman 2007), which estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$. Originally proposed by (Dempster 1972) under the name Covariance Selection, the framework has been expanded to include latent variables in (Chandrasekaran 2012) and more recently to jointly estimate multiple inverse covariance matrices, as seen in (Danaher 2013; Tomasi 2018). The GGLasso package supports the solution of a general formulation, encompassing significant special cases, including the single Graphical Lasso with latent variables, the Group, and the Fused Graphical Lasso.

By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, researchers can now quantify the sampling precision and the step-size dependent bias in configurational averaging. For harmonic oscillators, some methods yield exact configurational averages, potentially leading to enhanced performance in biomolecular simulations where bond stretches are significant. For general systems, an optimal method can be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. The simulations of alanine dipeptide reported here, both in vacuum and in a solvent, demonstrate that higher precision can be achieved without compromising computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps and maintaining the conformational exploration rate. This optimal scheme consistently outperforms other algorithms for molecular sampling, offering efficiency improvements of at least 25% in practical time steps in vacuum and reductions in configurational average errors by a factor of ten or more in solvated simulations at large time steps.

However, these simulations start relatively close to the merger, so it's essential to determine the initial conditions that accurately represent the binary and its environment at this point. In our research, we've been investigating how dark matter behaves around equal-mass black hole binaries, discovering a stable, long-lasting profile that emerges and grows over several orbits. Through the examination of extensive categories of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify the potential generalized global symmetries present and investigate the mechanisms by which they are circumvented. Key components of such effective field theories include generalized $\theta$-terms, which introduce non-linear interactions between axion fields and topological terms that are quadratic in gauge field strengths and which break a substantial portion of the global symmetries. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that the presence of such $\theta$-terms leads to an overly complicated potential for the axion fields, which is avoided when the generalized $\theta$-terms are integrated into the bulk. Furthermore, we reveal that the generalized $\theta$-terms result in a non-trivial Wess-Zumino term in the bulk, which is proportional to the four-dimensional Euler characteristic and leads to a shift in the charge of any monopole-like objects by one unit. As a consequence, the generalized $\theta$-terms induce a phase transition in the effective potential for the bulk scalar field, which we illustrate using a simplified model.

  Our objective is to minimize the number and intricacy of hardware and software components that a mobile user must trust to withstand malicious inputs. We propose a multi-domain hardware design consisting of isolated, statically-partitioned trust domains. To enable a program to temporarily access both processing and input/output functions exclusively and simultaneously, we introduce simple, formally-verified hardware components. For managing this hardware, we present OctopOS, an operating system comprising mutually distrustful subsystems.
  We have implemented a prototype of this system, combining hardware and OS on a CPU-FPGA board, and demonstrate that it incurs a minimal hardware cost compared to contemporary system-on-chip designs. For security-sensitive applications, this system significantly reduces the necessary trust compared to conventional trusted execution environments while achieving reasonable performance. For regular applications, performance is comparable to legacy systems.

Our adversary model assumes a sophisticated opponent who can manipulate the reward and transition at any step within an episode, but only up to a certain percentage of episodes. Our model is more aggressive than previous approaches. We initially demonstrated that no algorithm can find a significantly better policy than one that is slightly suboptimal, given our attack model. Notably, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can maintain robustness if the reward corruption is limited, and can find a near-optimal policy. To address unbounded reward corruption, we developed the Filtered Policy Gradient algorithm, which can find a nearly optimal policy despite significant corruption. multi-phonon physics, is being explored for its potential in metrology and on-chip communication, among other applications. Quantum acoustic resonators, or cavities, are being used to investigate multi-phonon phenomena through both theoretical and experimental means. We are studying a specific system consisting of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity. This setup has shown promise in producing interesting multi-phonon effects, but a previous model of the quantum dot as a two-level system was too restrictive. In this work, we instead consider a model that accounts for both bright and dark excitons in the quantum dot, with dark excitons being particularly useful due to their low decoherence rates. By fine-tuning the laser frequency and intensity, we are able to achieve giant Rabi oscillations between the vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles. Notably, we can create dark states in the quantum dot without the need for an external magnetic field, and in a scenario with losses, the system acts as a phonon gun capable of emitting N-phonon bundles. Our findings have implications for both phonon engineering and quantum acoustic metrology.

We model this system using a nearest-neighbour tight-binding model and find two distinct Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These Dirac cones can be modified through various perturbations applied to the Hamiltonian, which break the lattice symmetries. Initially, we introduce onsite potentials at lattice sites, observing the transformation of Dirac cones into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along high-symmetry paths. Subsequently, we apply a dimerization of the hopping terms and report a flow of Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone, characterised by quasi-hyperbolic curves. Additionally, we explore a potential implementation using CO atoms on a Cu(111) surface.

yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated through a process called quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. This occurs when a coherent state and a single-photon state are input into a beam splitter or parametric amplifier, and a single photon is detected in one of the output channels. The probabilities of successful detection differ depending on whether a beam splitter or parametric amplifier is used. We have also demonstrated that the SPCCSs generated by these two methods are identical, based on an analysis of their photon number distributions. Furthermore, we have thoroughly investigated the quantum properties of SPCCSs, including their non-Poissonian distribution, anti-bunching effect, quadrature squeezing effect, and the negativity of their Wigner function. These findings confirm that SPCCSs are non-Gaussian states that exhibit an abundance of non-classical behavior, and as such, they possess quantum advantages that can be leveraged for various technological applications.

integer linear programming has been proposed for designing chemical compounds with specific properties. This paper presents a new method based on this framework for predicting polymer structures. We introduce a novel representation of polymers as combinations of monomers and introduce new descriptors that capture their structural characteristics. Computational experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively predicts certain chemical properties of polymers, particularly when the monomers contain up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms.

Due to the infinite-dimensional nature of these problems and the lack of a general analytical solution, numerical methods are employed to find approximate solutions. We explore a common notation for the transcription step of direct optimization methods, focusing on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes. These methods are then applied to a case study, specifically addressing the ventilator shortage issue during the COVID-19 pandemic. CT scans can be very difficult due to low contrast, varying anatomy, and the presence of foreign objects. To overcome this, doctors often rely on additional information from endoscopic findings, medical history, and other imaging tests, which can be time-consuming and produce inconsistent results. This study investigates whether it's possible to automate the process of segmenting esophageal tumors from CT scans alone. To achieve this, we developed a fully automatic method based on convolutional neural networks, called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), which focuses on the most relevant features and regions. We tested this method on a large dataset of 792 scans from 288 patients with varying anatomies and conditions, and the results showed a high degree of accuracy with a simplified clinical workflow. Our code is available for public use.

This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method, to solve nonlinear problems like well logging. This method was paired with a robust strategy to handle geological uncertainties by breaking down resistivity formation evaluation tool (RFET) measurements into multiple ensemble members. Each member's measurement was artificially contaminated with noise at various levels, allowing the estimation of multiple scenarios concurrently. We demonstrated the efficacy of our approach by simulating and analyzing cases with noisy wireline measurements, positioning the well in a varied formation, and handling uncertainties in well logging, all of which were successfully handled with minimal computational resources, making it suitable for real-time operations.

One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling.

problems in arithmetic geometry, specifically to counting curves and their intersections in certain types of fields. We test our methods using a particular problem related to a type of curve called a plane quartic, and we look at how the geometry of this curve changes when we view it in different ways. We express the reasons why certain curves and their intersections may not behave well in terms of how their shapes change when viewed in different ways. We also show how to calculate the importance of certain curves and their intersections in terms of their shapes and the way they are defined. This allows us to confirm a prediction made by other mathematicians about the importance of certain types of curves and their intersections in certain types of fields. Our results rely on a theorem that helps us understand how the geometry of fields changes when we view them in different ways.

This paper introduces a new method for determining a mobile node's location in 802.15.4 (ZigBee) based networks using received signal strength indicators. We have developed and tested a range-based location algorithm that minimizes interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and the results of our hardware implementation match the ideal simulation results where an accuracy of less than 0.5 meters has been achieved.

To accurately analyze their electronic properties, researchers have turned to first-principles simulations. However, the existence of multiple stable polymorphs of these oxides presents a significant challenge when calculating and distinguishing their respective spectral features. To address this issue, researchers employed linear-response time-dependent density functional theory to investigate the energy loss function in the optical limit for various Ta$_2$O$_5$ polymorphs. Their findings indicate that experimental reflection energy loss signals can be explained by assuming that the $\gamma$-phase of Ta$_2$O$_5$ serves as the underlying structural model. Moreover, the inclusion of local field effects and spin-orbit coupling is essential for accurately computing the energy loss functions of this material. To further validate the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ polymorph as a model for experimental tantalum oxide, researchers used a Monte Carlo approach to calculate the reflection energy loss spectra, achieving a remarkable agreement with the experimental data.

We investigated whether this factor affects the online spread of misinformation, given that online interactions tend to be localized and decrease with distance. Analyzing over 8 million Reddit comments containing news links from 2016 to 2019 revealed that Reddit did not primarily facilitate misinformation, but rather operated as a supply-and-demand system where misinformation scaled linearly with user and connection numbers. However, we found that accounting for the heterogeneous distribution of Americans based on income, age, and education did not alter the result. Yet, examining subpopulations revealed that Reddit users in poorer, less educated areas more frequently shared news, including reputable sources, due to lower participation rates from higher-income, older individuals with lower connection densities. Consequently, poorer, less educated areas experienced higher relative circulation of all news, including credible sources.

Microwave Background (CMB) could serve as evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology (CCC) model, which proposes the universe undergoes cycles of expansion and contraction. These patterns include low-variance circles resulting from black hole mergers and Hawking points resulting from black hole evaporation. A recent study used machine learning software called HawkingNet to search for Hawking points in the CMB, but found no statistically significant evidence. Similarly, a high-resolution search for low-variance circles in the Planck and WMAP CMB data revealed no significant results after removing anomalies. However, the absence of distinct features in the CMB does not necessarily disprove CCC, as a large density of such patterns could produce a non-Gaussian fluctuation in the CMB. Interestingly, the real CMB sky exhibits significant local deviations from Gaussian noise on a local scale, according to the best-fit Lambda-CDM and COM PowerSpect CBM TT-full power spectra.

few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes often struggle due to the influence of outliers. The results were complemented with planetary injection tests. The parametric selection method yielded an RV RMS reduction of less than 10%, whereas the randomized selection method achieved a systematic improvement of over 50%, regardless of the activity level of the star examined. Object detectors that use deep learning process context differently in scene recognition. 
In this study, we classify object detectors into three types based on context usage: 
those that don't use context by isolating the input (RCNN), those that use partial context by isolating the feature map (two-stage methods), and those that use full context without any isolation (single-stage methods). 
We examine how context affects each deep detector category systematically. 
We create a dataset with controlled context variations and investigate context usage in deep detectors. 
Additionally, we assess the effect of removing background context and foreground objects on the MS COCO dataset and the Small Animal Dataset. 
Our results show that both single-stage and two-stage object detectors can leverage context due to their large receptive field. 
Therefore, selecting the best object detector depends on the specific application context.

This immunological hurdle has led to the development of desensitization techniques. Patients receiving incompatible kidneys face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, as well as post-operative complications such as delayed graft function, acute rejection, and mortality. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by comparing the outcomes of compatible and incompatible transplants using paired donations. A decision analysis framework is created to evaluate the effectiveness of incompatible kidney transplants based on compatibility level, with outcomes assessed through a literature review and a cohort study. The results indicate that end-stage kidney patients may benefit from receiving incompatible kidneys, with the optimal acceptance criteria depending on the level of incompatibility. Specifically, patients with a low risk of rejection can accept kidneys with a 50% higher HLA incompatibility than those with a higher risk. The expected survival probability of patients receiving incompatible kidneys is 0.726, compared to 0.854 for compatible kidneys. However, the majority of patients with end-stage kidney disease have a relatively low expected outcome from receiving incompatible kidneys. Therefore, reducing the risk of delayed graft function and post-operative complications is crucial to increase the percentage of patients benefiting from incompatible kidney transplants.

Our primary objective is to elucidate how the widespread use of embeddings in NLP is influenced by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. We utilize a mathematical framework to highlight the implicit assumptions regarding language structure inherent in this model. Our analysis reveals that Markovian assumptions provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are formed and how they capture frequentist synonyms. These assumptions enable the creation of generative models and an explicit analysis of the loss function commonly used in NLP techniques. Furthermore, we generate synthetic corpora with varying levels of structure and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of the word2vec algorithm in learning them. We also empirically evaluate the ability of these models to capture structures in a large corpus of financial news, spanning 12 years and comprising 42 million articles. Our analysis relies on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists, which are widely used in financial text analysis. We show that embeddings can mistakenly treat antonyms as frequentist synonyms, leading to the mixing of terms with opposing polarity. Additionally, we investigate the non-stationarity of the financial corpus, a phenomenon that has not been extensively documented in the literature. Our analysis involves time-series analysis of cosine similarity between groups of polarized words or company names, revealing that embeddings capture a complex mix of English semantics and word distributions that are difficult to disentangle.

Researchers have proposed a compositional interpretation of the extended Lambek Calculus using the compact closed category of FVect and linear maps, but this approach disregards the control modalities, limiting their role to the syntactic component. By building upon the directional density matrix semantics, we expand the type system's interpretation to include an additional spin density matrix space. Infective to Recovered (SIR) epidemic model on a social network is conducted. The underlying social network is modelled as an Erdos-Renyi random graph but, during an outbreak, individuals connected to infected neighbours may sever or re-establish connections. As the population grows, the model converges, revealing both the early branching process-like behaviour and the main phase of the epidemic process, which is equivalent to a deterministic model and a pair approximation model. The total number of individuals infected during a major outbreak is also studied, yielding a law of large numbers. Two key findings emerge: (i) the limiting fraction of infected individuals may exhibit a discontinuous jump from 0 to a positive value at the critical infection rate and (ii) when rewiring is restricted to uninfected individuals, the limiting fraction of infected individuals jumps from 0 to 1 at the critical infection rate.

Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness.

A new study proposes an alternative approach, which involves using new observable indicators to indirectly identify ultra-high energy photons through cosmic ray phenomena consisting of extensive air showers or primary cosmic rays observed simultaneously. This study utilizes simulations of ultra-high energy photons interacting with the Sun's magnetic field, incorporating essential modifications to the PRESHOWER program. The expected outcome of these interactions is the creation of cosmic ray ensembles in the form of extremely thin and elongated cascades of secondary photons spanning the entire cosmic ray energy spectrum. Upon entering the Earth's atmosphere, these cascades or their components can generate distinctive patterns of spatially correlated extensive air showers, which can also occur when primary ultra-high energy photons are not directed towards the Earth. The particle distributions within these multi-primary ultra-high energy photon footprints are anticipated to have thicknesses of approximately meters and elongations reaching hundreds of millions of kilometers, making them potentially observable with a global, multi-experiment approach, including the re-examination of historical data. The expected event rate exceeds the capabilities of even the largest cosmic ray observatories. The methods described in this report enable the simulation of observable quantities related to cosmic ray ensembles induced by ultra-high energy photons, including densities, energy spectra, and geographical orientations of particles at the top of the Earth's atmosphere.

-wide association studies (GWAS) can be difficult due to the complexity of available annotations. We have developed a statistical model that uses GWAS data to identify which types of genomic elements are more likely to influence a particular trait, incorporating multiple annotation types seamlessly. This model was applied to 18 human traits, such as blood cell characteristics, glucose and lipid levels, height, and Crohn's disease, analyzing 450 different annotations like genes, enhancers, and sensitive DNA sites in over a hundred tissues and cell types. Our results show that for various traits, only a small percentage of associated SNPs impact protein sequences, ranging from 2% for platelet volume to 20% for LDL cholesterol, and that certain traits are more likely to be associated with open or repressed chromatin. Furthermore, we discovered that cell-specific DNA sites are enriched in traits like platelet volume, specifically in the spleen. By integrating functional genomics into GWAS, we were able to increase the confidence in associated loci by around 5%.

To assess the feasibility of this test, I employed a specific method that involves analyzing only the velocity components within a specific plane in the sky. We have created numerical models of rotating low-mass stars to examine their ability to sustain nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates that result in significant deformation. Critical boundaries defining the conditions for sustainable hydrogen burning have been identified in terms of mass and central degeneracy for various levels of angular momentum. Our findings indicate that when the angular momentum surpasses a certain threshold, the critical boundary splits into two distinct regions with lower and higher degeneracy due to mass loss. Based on these results, we have modeled the thermal and mechanical evolution of substellar objects, taking into account cooling, mass loss, and angular momentum reduction. Two scenarios were considered: one involving external braking mechanisms, such as magnetized winds, which dictate the spin-down timescale, and the other where mass loss occurs through gravitational contraction, resulting in the formation of a ring or disc and subsequent shrinkage of the object.

groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. various AI tasks, particularly in visual recognition. Nonetheless, there are still several open issues, including the ability to process continuous visual data and the management of class imbalance in datasets. Current research tackles these problems separately, whereas they often coexist in real-world applications. In this study, we focus on the challenge of learning from incrementally imbalanced datasets, where the complexity of the deep model remains constant and the memory is limited to storing exemplars of past classes across incremental stages. Since the memory is restricted, older classes are learned from fewer images than new classes, exacerbating the initial class imbalance. Consequently, a bias towards new classes emerges, and we assess a range of score calibration methods to mitigate it. We conduct our evaluation using three datasets, two imbalance configurations, and three bounded memory sizes. The results demonstrate that most calibration methods yield beneficial effects, particularly in scenarios with lower bounded memory sizes, which are more relevant to practical applications. As a secondary contribution, we investigate the effect of removing the distillation component from the loss function of incremental learning algorithms and find that vanilla fine-tuning serves as a more robust foundation for imbalanced incremental learning methods.

research introduces a new technique called HyperDegrade, which combines existing methods with the use of multi-threading architectures.  In addition to this new technique, the study identifies the underlying causes of performance degradation through cache eviction and uncovers a previously unknown source of slowdown. The resulting slowdown is significantly higher than previous methods, leading to a finer time granularity for Flush+Reload attacks. The effectiveness of HyperDegrade is demonstrated on various Intel microarchitectures, yielding substantial slowdowns that achieve significant improvements over current state-of-the-art methods. To evaluate the effectiveness of performance degradation in side-channel amplification, the study proposes and evaluates metrics for assessing information leakage. The results show that HyperDegrade increases time granularity without compromising data quality. Furthermore, the study applies HyperDegrade to a real-world scenario, successfully leveraging performance degradation to enhance Flush+Reload attacks on an OpenSSL implementation that had proven resistant to data leakage through Flush+Reload. The proposed technique enables the recovery of sensitive information from memory regions originally deemed inaccessible by the attacker. The study also presents a novel method for identifying cryptographic contexts from performance degradation, allowing the extraction of secret keys from OpenSSL implementations that had previously been secure against Flush+Reload attacks. The newly developed performance degradation technique enables the amplification of side-channel attacks in real-world applications.

Tetralogy of Fallot patients primarily relies on ventricular volume and function according to current clinical guidelines. These biomarkers can be accurately assessed through 3D cardiac magnetic resonance image segmentation. Recent studies have shown that U-Net architectures have achieved impressive results on various datasets. However, in real-world clinical settings, data sets are more diverse and influenced by individual pathologies, scanner properties, and limited training data for rare conditions like Tetralogy of Fallot. This work investigates two aspects: the accuracy gap when training models on one dataset (ACDC) and applying them to another (TOF), and whether similar results can be achieved when applying models to a more heterogeneous dataset. Multiple deep learning models were trained and evaluated using four-fold cross-validation, demonstrating that models can achieve excellent results within a single dataset but struggle with overfitting when applied to other pathologies, resulting in significantly reduced dice scores for both left and right ventricles.

Pyramid Networks (FPNs), have been facing a long-standing challenge. FPNs generally improve detection performance but often at the expense of large-scale objects. This paper investigates the impact of FPNs on detection frameworks from an optimization perspective. It identifies the root cause of the suppressed performance of large-scale objects as the creation of improper back-propagation paths after integrating FPNs. This limitation restricts each level of the backbone network to focus on objects within a specific scale range. To address this issue, two strategies are proposed. Firstly, auxiliary objective functions are introduced to enable each backbone level to receive signals from various-scale objects during training. Secondly, a more rational approach to constructing the feature pyramid is proposed to eliminate irrational back-propagation paths. Experimental results on the COCO benchmark validate the analysis and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, achieving significant improvements of over 2% in various detection frameworks.

Unfortunately, current methodologies lack a systematic approach to assess these extreme assumptions due to complex copula and marginal forms. These tools allow us to derive explicit formulas for approximating extreme cases of a specific type of model, including the distribution of a tail event and a key metric of asymptotic independence. Although humans can easily sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the extent to which current machine learning models possess this capability remains uncertain. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the signal-recycled Michelson design where the usual arm configuration is replaced with an additional optical path that integrates the light from the interacting beams. Given an irreducible simple algebraic group G and a Borel subgroup B, consider an irreducible subgroup P containing B, and let P' be its derived group. A theorem by Richardson states that the algebra of P semi-invariants is multiplicity-free. A linear subvariety e+V that induces an isomorphism between the algebra of P semi-invariants and the algebra of e+V is called a Weierstrass section. In this work, a Weierstrass section is constructed in type A, with a focus on its application rather than its construction. The nilfibre relative to the action of P is denoted by N, and it is shown that a point e in N is contained in a unique irreducible component C of N. Using the structure of the Weierstrass section, an explicit description of C is given as a B saturation set, which is a subset of the form B.u, where u is a subalgebra of the Lie algebra of the nilradical of B. However, this subalgebra may not be complemented, and thus the closure of B.u may not be an orbital variety closure. It is demonstrated that C may not contain a dense P orbit, and this is shown through a theoretical analysis, with an example in A10.

Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, but the current research extends beyond this limitation by exploring a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where data samples are inherently interdependent. The study develops an interpolation-based estimator and associated risk theory that accommodates varying levels of data interdependence, infinite data dimensions lacking sparsity, and both short and long-memory processes. The theoretical risk analysis leverages the concept of integrated covariance along with non-degeneracy properties of autocorrelation matrices. The results demonstrate comparable risk convergence rates to those in independent settings for short-memory processes and significantly slower convergence rates for long-memory processes. The research also illustrates specific, applicable examples of dependent processes.

Experiments conducted on DPSs from various manufacturers revealed that resonance can be achieved in multiple devices, causing a significant change in pressure readings. To mitigate this threat, countermeasures are proposed to prevent such an attack.

Active learning algorithms are crucial in large-scale settings where labeling costs are high, and leveraging unlabeled data is essential for improving model performance. The effectiveness of self-supervised pretraining in utilizing unlabeled data is a significant factor in achieving better model performance. By combining active learning with self-supervised pretraining, one can efficiently utilize unlabeled data and selectively train on informative samples. 

In this study, we examine the combination of active learning and self-supervised pretraining on the ImageNet dataset and find that the performance on small datasets does not accurately represent the performance on larger datasets like ImageNet due to class imbalance. We discovered that selecting more challenging samples through active learning does not necessarily lead to better performance and that the benefit of active learning is largely eliminated when starting from a well-initialized pretrained model. The existing literature does not fully demonstrate the effectiveness of active learning on large datasets like ImageNet due to the high performance of baseline models. To accurately evaluate active learning on large datasets, it is necessary to assess the method on a variety of algorithms, as some methods may be specifically designed to work well with particular neural network architectures or datasets.

The annealed large deviation principle for the empirical process of words involves a rate function that is the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words relative to the reference distribution of words. In a previous study, the quenched large deviation principle was derived for renewal times with an algebraic tail, resulting in a rate function consisting of two terms: the annealed rate function and a term proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters, obtained by concatenating words and randomizing the origin. This study aims to extend both large deviation principles to non-i.i.d. letter sequences by demonstrating that they remain valid under a condition known as summable variation. The resulting rate functions are specific relative entropies with respect to the reference distributions of words and letters, which are not necessarily i.i.d. This requires several approximation arguments to achieve the extension.

This technology utilizes passive reflective elements capable of adjusting the phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization of incoming waveforms. Given its desirable properties, the characteristics of wireless channels can be manipulated to meet specific signal requirements, holding great promise for radar applications. This paper lays the theoretical groundwork for integrating IRS into radar systems and explores its potential to improve target parameter estimation. Specifically, we examine the deployment of IRS in scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link is weak or obstructed by obstacles. We demonstrate that IRS can establish a virtual, non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link between the radar and target, leading to enhanced radar performance. Numerical simulations reveal that the effectiveness of this virtual link in estimating target parameters is improved when the LOS link is significantly weaker than the NLOS link, with a relative strength ratio of approximately $10^{-1}$.

In software testing, mutation analysis is a widely adopted method for evaluating test quality by assessing the ability to detect artificial bugs; if a set of tests fails to detect such mutations, it will also fail to detect actual bugs. This method encompasses various coverage measures and can be tailored to suit specific needs. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is hindered by the need for independent evaluation of fuzzers, which hinders a fair comparison of fuzzing techniques and artifacts. This paper introduces an extensive mutation analysis framework for fuzzers, encompassing multiple coverage metrics and mutation techniques, allowing for the measurement of fuzzer performance and comparison of effectiveness. To address the issue of evaluating fuzzer-produced inputs, the framework incorporates various input quality metrics, including the ability to measure the reachability of fuzzer-generated test cases. Additionally, the framework enables the independent evaluation of fuzzers, facilitating the comparison of fuzzer performance, such as the percentage of detected mutations and failures reached. Through the application of this framework to well-known fuzzers and mutations in programs, including binary, script, and network-based programs, we demonstrate its capabilities and present recommendations for using mutation analysis to evaluate fuzzyers.

In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. This unpredictability makes effective optimization challenging, particularly when resources are limited. Recent studies have focused on mitigating the random fluctuations in CV performance estimates by employing multiple random partitions. ysics is the common envelope phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped by the outer layer of one of them. The interactions between the stars and the surrounding layer cause the orbit to contract. This phase can ultimately lead to the merging of the stars or a subsequent series of interactions. Mergers involving compact objects, such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes, can produce a range of spectacular astrophysical events, including supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and gravitational waves. Due to the diversity of initial conditions and the complexity of the processes involved, predicting the final state of common envelope phases is challenging. In large-scale calculations, such as population synthesis models, conservation laws are often employed. This study develops a novel approach to utilizing angular momentum to derive a simplified formula for the final orbital separation in common envelope phases, offering advantages in the study of binary and multiple star systems, particularly in the context of potential mergers. This work primarily focuses on common envelope phases in binary star systems, while a companion paper extends the methodology to more complex multiple star systems.

we've analyzed the large-scale structure of ionized and molecular gas in the starburst galaxy IRAS08339+6517, located 500 parsecs away. Our study investigates the connection between star-forming gas outflows and related star formation rates. We found that the mass flux of these outflows is directly proportional to the galaxy's star formation rate, suggesting that outflows are an essential process in regulating gas supply and further indicating that dust attenuation has a limited effect on this relationship. These findings are consistent with models predicting that outflows are a response to the disruption of gas by short-lived radioactive decay products. Our results highlight the significance of constraining dust attenuation when estimating outflow masses. Moreover, our analysis shows that dust attenuation has a minor effect on the ratio of dust and gas masses, resulting in an approximately 10% decrease in this ratio for galaxies similar to IRAS08339+6517, which is consistent with the average ratio for local star-forming galaxies.

Recently, Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO) has successfully addressed these difficulties by utilizing probabilistic models. SBO achieves fast convergence by breaking down the parameter space using contextual information from system experts. However, the complexity of building probabilistic models has limited its widespread adoption. To overcome this hurdle, we introduce BoAnon, a SBO framework that learns the system's structure from its logs. BoAnon provides a user-friendly interface for experts to incorporate their knowledge about the system's behavior and component dependencies. By combining the learned structure with expert-provided information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model that enables the optimizer to discover efficient configurations more quickly than other methods. In a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a significant improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7 times better performance than the default architecture. time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) lies in maintaining the integrity of specific properties inherent to the continuous solution, such as underlying conservation laws or geometric structures. Researchers have been studying structure-preserving discretisation schemes for a considerable amount of time, including verifying that conventional methods retain these properties and proposing innovative schemes that achieve both high accuracy and exact preservation of certain properties of the underlying differential equation. However, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, these schemes have a significant drawback - their ability to preserve structure relies on the exact solution of the systems of equations defining each time-step in the discrete scheme. Although this is feasible for small systems, it becomes impractical for large linear systems resulting from typical discretisation of space-time PDEs. This paper proposes an adjustment to the flexible generalised minimum residual (FGMRES) iteration that enforces selected constraints on approximate numerical solutions, and demonstrates its application to both conservation laws and dissipative systems.

Our research focuses on the early stages of superbubble evolution, including pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae. We aimed to investigate the growth of dust grains within orbiting dusty clumps and the superbubble's swept-up supershell, as well as the survival of dust grains produced by sequential supernovae. Our model takes into account the gravitational potential of the star cluster and the self-gravity of the parent cloud, as well as radiative cooling and a state-of-the-art population synthesis model for the coeval cluster. Our findings show that in massive molecular clouds hosting a super star cluster, dust grain growth increases the dust mass at a rate of approximately 4.8 times 10 to the negative 5 solar masses per year during the first 2.5 million years. Furthermore, pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae contribute significantly to the superbubble's dust budget, resulting in the creation of massive amounts of dust without relying on a top-heavy initial mass function. This process is consistent with the large dust mass observed in galaxies during the early stages of cosmic reionization.

However, existing benchmarks, such as the nuScenes dataset, do not adequately address this problem as they only evaluate performance up to a certain distance. This is partly due to the difficulty in obtaining far-field 3D annotations, particularly from lidar sensors that often produce few point returns for distant objects. Moreover, current 3D detection metrics employ a one-size-fits-all approach, which is inconsistent with the varying tolerances required for human vision and stereo disparities. As a result, the Far3Det task is not thoroughly analyzed. For instance, the conventional wisdom that high-resolution RGB sensors are vital for detecting far-away objects is contradicted by the current benchmark leaderboards, which show lidar-based methods ranking higher. To address this, we developed a method to create a well-annotated far-field validation set from the nuScenes dataset and proposed a Far3Det evaluation protocol. We also explored various 3D detection methods in the Far3Det task and demonstrated that high-resolution RGB sensors significantly improve detection in the far-field. Furthermore, we introduced a simple yet effective fusion method that combines detections from RGB and lidar detectors, which outperforms state-of-the-art 3D detectors in the far-field. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/Qingyuong/NuSc

the potential energy surface (PES) of molecules, which represents their energy levels in relation to their nuclear positions. Nevertheless, calculating this data is complex due to the vast number of ground states and the high-dimensional nature of the PES, making it difficult to prepare the required quantum states. This research introduces a novel approach using a generative quantum machine learning model that enables the preparation of quantum states at any point on the PES by training the model with quantum data consisting of ground-state wavefunctions associated with various classical nuclear coordinates. A classical neural network is employed to convert nuclear coordinates into quantum parameters for a variational quantum circuit, which is optimized using a fidelity loss function. Our method demonstrates efficient gradient evaluation and effectively prepares wavefunctions for hydrogen chains, water, and beryllium hydride, showcasing its ability to achieve high overlap with ground states using a limited number of training points. Furthermore, this research establishes theoretical limitations by showing that learning across an avoided crossing with a small number of samples would violate Grover's lower bound, and it also proves lower bounds on the amount of quantum data required to learn a locally optimal neural network function using arguments from quantum Fisher information. Ultimately, this work highlights the significance of quantum chemistry as a potential application for quantum machine learning.

However, obtaining precise annotations for scene flow using LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is time-consuming and labor-intensive. To address this issue, we propose a scene flow benchmark and a novel self-supervised training framework. The benchmark comprises datasets that progressively increase in complexity, from a single moving object to real-world environments. We use our benchmark to evaluate the performance of our proposed setup and various baselines, finding that our method successfully preserves motion coherence and local geometry, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail to achieve this. This property was first studied in the 1970s by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist, who combined three key properties: matchings, Hamiltonicity, and edge-colourings. This work focuses on cubic graphs, examining how perfect matchings relate to proper 3-edge-colourings and whether these graphs can be classified as even-2-factorable, meaning all their 2-factors consist of even cycles. Since bipartite cubic graphs are trivially even-2-factorable, we concentrate on non-bipartite cubic graphs. Having the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property is a sufficient but not necessary condition for a cubic graph to be even-2-factorable. This research aims to introduce a family of even-2-factorable non-bipartite cubic graphs, called papillon graphs, and determine the parameters for which they possess the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property or are even-2-factorable, also showing that no two papillon graphs with different parameters are isomorphic.

To address this limitation, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI) were developed. WRI and ESI differ from FWI in that they relax the need for accurate wave equation satisfaction during iteration, and instead, utilize non-physical sources to match observed data. Formulated within the same mathematical framework, WRI and ESI are essentially weighted versions of FWI. To efficiently solve the normal equation, the conjugate gradient method is employed, and both time and frequency domain wave equation solvers are feasible. Nevertheless, the main challenge lies in the enormous storage requirements for time-domain wavefields during iterations. To mitigate this issue, two possible workarounds involve extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data instead of wavefields.

Utilizing binary phase shifts from a thermally stable nonlinear resonator, we achieved a degree of squeezing exceeding 6 dB. This allowed us to construct an all-optical circulator that successfully isolated the input light from the output, even in the presence of various linear and nonlinear losses. The device's fidelity and isolation efficiency were tested with single photons and weak coherent states, demonstrating reliability and versatility. Our approach provides a novel path for designing compact, stable optical isolators and circulators using the unique properties of squeezed light.

Researchers have developed empirical relations that use accessible data to estimate stellar properties, often in the form of non-linear functions. However, Bayesian modeling requires the opposite approach. This article introduces a novel Bayesian framework that can simultaneously apply multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the mass, luminosity, radius, and effective temperature of field age M-dwarfs. The framework includes a new mass-radius relation for M-dwarfs with a scatter of 3.1% at fixed mass. The study also introduces the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS) and applies the methodology to nearby low-mass stars with available ultraviolet spectroscopic data. These stars are of interest as exoplanet hosts or benchmarks for stellar activity in various wavelengths. By using the field MUSS stars, the study defines the low-mass main sequence in the solar neighborhood through Gaussian Process regression. The results reveal a feature in the GP derivative at 0.337 ± 0.026 M⊙, indicating where the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample transitions from fully to partly convective interiors.

This paper introduces a decision-making process to determine whether a given function is computable and, if so, to create a Turing machine that computes it. Two key theories attempt to explain this animacy continuum: the visual categorization theory proposes that it is driven by the presence of animal-specific characteristics, while the agency theory suggests that it is rooted in how animals are perceived as agents. In this study, we investigated these hypotheses by creating a stimulus set that isolated visual categorizability and agency, and then used fMRI to analyze how they contributed to the animacy continuum in the ventral temporal cortex. Our results indicate that both visual categorizability and agency play distinct roles in shaping the animacy continuum, and that together they fully account for its complexity. Furthermore, our data show that visual categorizability and agency have different spatial representations within the ventral temporal cortex, with visual categorizability localized more posteriorly than agency. These findings demonstrate that multiple factors, including agency, contribute to the organization of the animacy continuum in the ventral temporal cortex, and that different cognitive principles can drive organized representations in this region.

We conduct novel research to identify and attribute the sources of bias in statistical predictions of Bperp, employing a neural network regression model called Magneto-Picasso. Initially, we diagnose the bias in prediction residuals, observing a linear trend in all datasets examined, despite varying input image characteristics. Subsequently, we investigate and propose solutions to the identified bias sources, which arise from: (1) over-smoothing at high-kappa values, likely caused by underestimating the local gradient; (2) incorrect local orientation in relation to the angle of the magnetic field; (3) noise amplification in areas with low signal-to-noise ratio; and (4) systematic differences between different flux recovery values. To mitigate these issues, we introduce a simple pre-processing technique called linear adjustment pre-processing (LAP), which stabilizes the prediction residuals, enabling more accurate predictions. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of LAP in multiple datasets, both in synthetic and real-world scenarios, and show that accounting for bias in predictive models can lead to more reliable magnetic field inferrals.

The custom pipeline developed to mitigate contamination enabled the identification of 6097 clusters, representing the largest sample of young star cluster radii to date. The study reveals that a significant number of galaxies exhibit a shared distribution of cluster radii, peaking at approximately 3 pc. Furthermore, a distinct mass-radius relationship was observed, where the effective radius is directly proportional to mass at a rate of 0.24. The research also indicates that the majority of LEGUS clusters are gravitationally bound, particularly at older ages or higher masses. The study's findings also include the cluster density and surface density distributions, which display a substantial scatter that diminishes with cluster age. The youngest clusters were found to have a typical surface density of 100 solar masses per square parsec.

By analyzing the data, we identified areas of the galaxy that have been significantly enriched in certain chemicals, likely the result of massive stars exploding as supernovae. omechanical behavior in unfilled polymers undergoing strain-induced crystallization. The crystallization process significantly affects a polymer's mechanical and thermal properties, necessitating consideration in manufacturing and application design. To comprehensively capture its effects, the proposed model employs a novel approach that involves decomposing the deformation gradient into three components and utilizes the Coleman-Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle for material modeling. The chosen framework yields equations capable of simulating crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic tensile testing. The resulting boundary value problem, which includes linear momentum and energy balance, serves as the basis for numerical implementation in a finite element method (FEM) code. The paper concludes with numerical examples illustrating microstructure evolution and temperature distribution in various material samples.

doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis.

Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple tasks at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback.

This was initially discovered by analyzing the noise kernels associated with the stress-energy tensor of quantum fields. In this study, we revisit this phenomenon using a quantum thermodynamics approach, examining the heat capacity and quantum compressibility of model spacetimes filled with a quantum field at both high and low temperatures. The heat capacity, in particular, is a measure of energy density fluctuations, and a ratio exceeding unity raises questions about the validity of the canonical distribution. Similarly, a system's compressibility is a criterion for the validity of the grand canonical ensemble. We derive the free energy density and calculate the heat capacity and compressibility for various spacetime geometries, including 2D Casimir space, 2D Einstein cylinder, and 4D Einstein universe, as well as higher-dimensional Einstein universes. This comprehensive analysis enables us to investigate the thermodynamic stability of quantum matter fields and make observations about the compatibility conditions for the coexistence of quantum fields and spacetimes, a fundamental issue in the intersection of quantum mechanics and gravity.

Focusing on the deep-inelastic scattering regime, we establish the corresponding moment sum rules for the structural functions and demonstrate that these moments are determined by the thermal expectation value of twist-two operators. unclonable encryption, a technique that prevents an adversary from creating multiple ciphertexts decrypting to the same original message. This notion is revisited, and the following advancements are presented:

  - Enhanced Security: Previous constructions either offered one-time security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. New constructions provide unclonable encryption schemes with semantic security, meeting minimal cryptographic requirements for both public-key and private-key settings.
  - Improved Lower Bound and Generalized Construction: The information-theoretic one-time secure construction by Broadbent and Lord was analyzed, revealing a success probability of $0.85^n$. A generalized construction based on a broader class of monogamy of entanglement games is proposed, along with cloning attacks achieving probabilities of $0.71^n$ and $0.75^n$ against specific schemes.
  - Implications for Copy-Protection: Unclonable encryption satisfying a stronger property, unclonable-indistinguishability, implies copy-protection for a specific class of unlearnable functions. Although current encryption schemes do not meet this criterion, this connection offers a new path to construct copy-protection mechanisms.

The presence of lattice relaxation in the sample causes the flat band to blend with remote valence bands, leading to significant differences in the contribution of interband transitions to the plasmon dispersion and energy. Under conditions where only intraband transitions within the doped flat band are considered, low-damped and quasi-flat plasmons arise. Conversely, a $\sqrt q$ plasmon dispersion is observed when interband transitions between the flat band and remote bands are also taken into account. The plasmon energies can be adjusted through twist angles and doping levels. However, in rigid samples without lattice relaxation, both lower-energy quasi-flat plasmons and higher-energy interband plasmons can coexist. For highly doped rigid samples, enhanced interband transitions can suppress the quasi-flat plasmons. Our study highlights the importance of two key factors, the isolated flat band and a suitable hole-doping level, for observing the low-damped and quasi-flat plasmon mode in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides. The findings of this research may provide valuable insights for studying plasmon-mediated superconductivity in these materials in the future.

an expansive outflow of material, often funneled by magnetic fields into surrounding magnetospheres. The powerful winds of massive stars are generated by the scattering of radiative energy, whereas in smaller stars like the Sun, weaker mass loss occurs due to the thermal expansion of heated coronas. In exoplanets orbiting these low-mass stars, radiative heating and wind interaction can cause atmospheric expansion or erosion. Stellar magnetospheres form internally due to wind trapping, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by external stellar wind impacts. However, in both cases, stress can trigger magnetic reconnection, producing observable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to provide an overview of the underlying physics of these processes, highlighting their similarities and differences in stars and planets.

This study centers on agreement prediction in Basque, serving as a case study for a task requiring an implicit comprehension of sentence structure and the acquisition of a complex yet systematic morphological system. As the planet rapidly approaches its star, its surface temperature jumps from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will study the planet's atmosphere as it interacts with its star's intense energy. To accurately interpret these observations, a comprehensive model of the planet's atmosphere is necessary, which requires understanding how the planet heats up as it approaches its star. They also studied how the planet's atmosphere responds to the changing heat input as it moves through its orbit. The results of these simulations will be used to develop a model that predicts the observable signs of heat escaping the planet's atmosphere, which will be tested against new observations. This research will provide a new understanding of how the planet's atmosphere changes as it moves through its orbit and how it responds to the intense energy from its star. By studying this planet, researchers will gain new insights into the fundamental processes that occur in atmospheres of planets that pass in front of their stars.

To reduce radiation exposure, PET scans can be taken with lower doses or shorter acquisition times, but this can compromise image quality. Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the creation of high-quality PET images from low-quality scans, often in conjunction with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data.  Existing deep learning methods typically segment PET and MRI images before feeding them to a reconstruction network.  However, these methods fail to utilize the temporal information inherent in PET scans, which can be extracted from kinetic data.  To address this limitation, we have developed a novel deep learning framework that incorporates temporal information and relies on the interdependence between PET and MRI imaging techniques.  Our framework, called the temporal pet-mri unified transformer (TP-MIT), leverages the advantages of the transformer architecture to effectively combine multiple types of data, and is particularly well-suited for low-dose PET scans.  We have evaluated the performance of our method on a public dataset and shown that it can produce high-quality PET images from low-quality scans and MRI data, with results comparable to traditional reconstruction methods.  We believe that our framework offers a superior approach to enhancing PET image quality, particularly in scenarios where radiation exposure needs to be minimized.

This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT.

searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through the SETI initiative, with a key focus on identifying Dyson Spheres - hypothetical structures surrounding stars that harness their energy for advanced civilizations. This study examines the feasibility of constructing a Dyson Sphere around a black hole, exploring six potential energy sources, including the cosmic microwave background, Hawking radiation, and relativistic jets. Our analysis indicates that collecting energy from an accretion disk, which can reach luminosities of $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$, could be sufficient to support a Type II civilization. Furthermore, incorporating other forms of energy from relativistic jets could increase the total energy collection by approximately fivefold. Considering the detectability of a Dyson Sphere, our results suggest that such a structure surrounding a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way could be observable in the ultraviolet, optical, near-infrared, and mid-infrared spectrums via waste heat radiation, potentially identifiable using current telescopes and techniques such as spectral energy distribution fitting and radial velocity measurements.

This can be achieved through active or passive monitoring methods. The latter involves observing real network traffic, which is more cost-effective and allows for more accurate results. However, this approach is hindered by the rapid growth of traffic volumes. To overcome this limitation, high-speed traffic processing technologies such as Non-Blocking Table-Routed (NBT) devices can be utilized to facilitate faster and more efficient traffic monitoring. Research has shown that selecting an appropriate filling pattern and recirculation scheme for a multi-pass energy recovery linac can significantly influence the interactions between the beam and RF system. , cutting-edge long-baseline neutrino experiments heavily rely on accurate models of neutrino interactions with atomic nuclei. These models contribute significantly to the overall systematic uncertainty due to the limited ability of existing detectors to detect final state neutrons. Next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments will incorporate three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers in their near detectors, which boast superior timing resolution and fine granularity. This technology enables the measurement of neutron kinetic energy in neutrino interactions on a per-event basis, thus providing valuable data to refine neutrino interaction models and improve neutrino energy reconstruction. Prototypes of these detectors have been tested at the neutron beamline at Los Alamos National Laboratory, exposing them to neutron energies between 0 and 800 MeV in 2019 and 2020. To validate their neutron detection capabilities, the total neutron-scintillator cross section was measured and compared to external data, yielding a value of 0.36 $\pm$ 0.05 barn between 98 and 688 MeV.

how temperature influences the attraction between tiny, chondritic particles. We observed that their surface energy decreased by approximately five times as the temperature increased. In this study, we investigated the effect of surface moisture on these particles. Typically, in a laboratory setting, multiple variables change simultaneously when exploring the overall adhesion between particles, so we decided to experimentally evaluate their combined impact. We focused initially on the role of surface energy, which we determined to decrease by approximately five times as the temperature increased, remaining relatively unaffected by the amount of water present. Next, we calculated the tensile strength of the aggregate material, which increased by approximately ten times as the water content increased, regardless of the temperature. Finally, we used these two factors to model the overall adhesion between particles, finding that their combined impact is mostly insensitive to temperature and water. This is consistent with the findings of other researchers. However, our results suggest that the relative importance of different factors varies depending on the specific type of particles being studied.

Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness.

In this work, we calculate the one-loop six-gluon amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, focusing on the central next-to-multi-Regge kinematic limit. Our results show that the dispersive part of this amplitude factorises into the two-gluon central emission vertex, allowing us to derive the one-loop two-gluon central emission vertex for all helicity configurations within this theory.
